approachQuestion.prompt:
Compare two inventories with multiplicity

Input: two arrays left and right containing inventory identifiers. Return true exactly when both arrays contain the same identifiers with the same multiplicities, regardless of order. Example 1: left = [4, 7, 4, 9], right = [9, 4, 7, 4] → true. Example 2: left = [3, 3, 8], right = [3, 8, 8] → false, even though their distinct identifier sets match. Example 3: left = [], right = [] → true.
constraints: The arrays have equal length, and −1,000,000,000 ≤ each identifier ≤ 1,000,000,000.
Return one boolean; do not mutate either input.
Assume integer-key hash table lookups and insertions have expected amortized constant cost under an ordinary non-adversarial distribution; this is not a worst-case guarantee.

options.text: Count each identifier from left in a map. Scan right, rejecting a missing or exhausted count and otherwise decrementing it. Return true only if the scan finishes with all counts consumed.
options.feedback: The map preserves multiplicities while order is ignored; decrementing detects both missing identifiers and too many copies.

options.text: Sort copies of both arrays and compare corresponding values.
options.feedback: Sorting groups equal identifiers, so equal sorted arrays are exactly multiset-equal. A frequency map can avoid sorting while preserving the same multiplicity information.

options.text: For each value in left, search right for one equal position not used by an earlier match; return true if every value gets a match.
options.feedback: This can be correct, but repeatedly searching for an unused match is brute force; the same values can be matched while consuming counts in a map.

options.text: Build one set from each array and compare the two sets.
options.feedback: Sets discard multiplicity. For left = [3, 3, 8] and right = [3, 8, 8], the sets are equal although the inventories are not.

feedback.reason: Ignore ordering while preserving every occurrence; membership alone cannot tell whether counts match.
details: Build a map of identifier counts from the left array. Then process the right array: reject immediately if an identifier has no remaining count; otherwise decrement that count. When the scan finishes, equal input lengths ensure that all counts have been consumed exactly when the inventories match.
Decrementing available copies distinguishes [2,2,5] from [2,5,5]. Equal lengths plus no over-consumption imply all counts are exhausted; a set cannot enforce this multiplicity condition.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Count the first inventory and consume counts” shown after your first answer, choose its expected running time and auxiliary-space pair under this explicit model: For this question, assume integer-key hash operations take expected amortized O(1) time under a non-adversarial hash distribution. State expected time on that basis; do not interpret it as an unconditional worst-case guarantee. Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input arrays and the returned scalar/pair, but includes every map/set and temporary structure.
constraints: For this question, assume integer-key hash operations take expected amortized O(1) time under a non-adversarial hash distribution. State expected time on that basis; do not interpret it as an unconditional worst-case guarantee. Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input arrays and the returned scalar/pair, but includes every map/set and temporary structure.

options.text: Expected O(n) time; O(u) auxiliary space, where u is the number of distinct identifiers in left.
Guaranteed worst-case O(n) time for every hash distribution; O(u) auxiliary space.
O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Scan both inventories and retain left-side multiplicities.
details: The map counts left once, then each right value performs one remaining-count lookup and decrement. Equal-length input makes complete consumption sufficient.

Expected O(n): n map updates from left and n lookups/decrements from right, each expected amortized O(1) under the stated hash model. Adversarial collisions can increase ordinary hash-map worst-case time; guaranteed worst-case linear time is not claimed.
O(u) map entries for distinct identifiers in left. Both supplied arrays and the boolean result are excluded.
“Expected O(n) time; O(u) auxiliary space, where u is the number of distinct identifiers in left.”: Correct under the explicit expected/amortized hash-operation assumption.
“Guaranteed worst-case O(n) time for every hash distribution; O(u) auxiliary space.”: Incorrect because standard hash maps do not guarantee constant-time operations for every collision distribution.
“O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary space.”: Incorrect for the fixed count-map method; it does not sort.
“O(n²) time; O(1) auxiliary space.”: Incorrect for the fixed method; it processes each supplied occurrence a constant expected number of times.
